**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Paibon Textile Care Partners, LLC / acquisition of Kestrin Linen Services, Inc.: pre-Closing issues in the deal documents
**Matter:** s9-m0001

---

## 1. Summary

Paibon Textile Care Partners, LLC (Buyer) is acquiring all of the shares of Kestrin Linen Services, Inc. (the Company) from Zanoul Holdings, Inc. (Seller).

- **Purchase Price:** **$42,000,000** (SPA §2.1).
- **Indemnity Escrow Amount:** **$4,200,000**, held by Ostrander Trust Company, N.A. (SPA §2.2(b)). This figure is also the general indemnity cap (SPA §9.6(a)).
- **Signing:** June 1, 2026.
- **Closing:** scheduled for **August 14, 2026** (SPA §3.1).
- **Outside date:** September 30, 2026 (SPA §8.1(b)).

I reviewed all four documents in the folder:
- the Stock Purchase Agreement (SPA);
- the agreed-form Bill of Sale;
- the Indemnity Escrow Agreement, dated July 28, 2026; and
- the closing-logistics email thread, which runs through August 12, 2026.

Five issues need attention before Closing. Each one either reduces what Paibon can recover after Closing or removes value Paibon expected to get. **The issues are ranked by severity, with the highest-priority item first:**

| # | Issue | Where | Bottom line |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Escrow "sole source" clause removes the SPA cap carve-outs | Escrow Agt §6.4; SPA §§9.5, 9.6(b), 11.9 | Recovery for title, tax and other "uncapped" claims is limited to the $4.2M escrow. After the escrow is released, recovery is zero. |
| 2 | Larkfield change-of-control consent is neither a condition nor indemnified | SPA Sch. 4.10, §7.2(d)/Sch. 7.2(d), §9.2(f) | Paibon must close without the largest customer's consent and has no indemnity if Larkfield terminates. |
| 3 | Environmental representations expire before the Phase II must be finished | SPA §§9.1(b), 6.7 | Survival ends Feb 10, 2027. The Phase II deadline is May 11, 2027. Contamination the Phase II finds is likely time-barred. |
| 4 | Section 338(h)(10) election notice window has closed | SPA §6.11 | The window closed July 16, 2026, and the folder contains no notice. Seller's obligation to join the election has lapsed, and the basis step-up is lost unless the SPA is amended. |
| 5 | Escrow Agreement's governing law and forum conflict with the SPA | Escrow Agt §10.4; SPA §§11.6, 11.7 | New York law and Manhattan courts apply to the escrow; Delaware law and the Court of Chancery apply to indemnity claims. This creates a risk of split proceedings and of the escrow agent not recognising a Delaware judgment. |

Lower-priority drafting and closing points, missing items and open facts are covered in Sections 3 and 4.

**Timing.** All of the fixes below require Seller's written agreement (SPA §11.3). The escrow fixes also require Ostrander's signature (Escrow Agt §10.2). Our leverage is greatest before funds move on August 14. If Closing has already taken place by the time this memo is acted on, each fix becomes a post-closing amendment and our leverage drops sharply. Please confirm the status.

---

## 2. Issues ranked by consequence

### Issue 1: Escrow Agreement §6.4 makes the escrow the only source of recovery, which removes the SPA's carve-outs for Fundamental Representations and Pre-Closing Taxes

**Where it appears**
- **Escrow Agreement §6.4.** "The Escrow Funds shall be the sole and exclusive source of recovery for all claims of the Buyer Indemnitees under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement, except claims for actual fraud."
- **Escrow Agreement §6.5.** If the Escrow Funds are insufficient, Buyer receives only what is available.
- **SPA §9.6(a).** Caps liability for general representation claims at the Indemnity Escrow Amount ($4,200,000).
- **SPA §9.6(b).** Carves out Fundamental Representations, Pre-Closing Taxes and fraud. Those claims are recoverable up to the full **$42,000,000** Purchase Price.
- **SPA §9.5.** Losses are paid first from the escrow and then "directly by Seller."
- **SPA §11.9.** The SPA generally prevails over Ancillary Documents, "except that the Escrow Agreement shall control with respect to the release of and recovery from the Escrow Funds."

**Why it matters for Paibon**
- **The precedence clause does not help Paibon here.** The §11.9 exception expressly gives the Escrow Agreement control over recovery from the Escrow Funds, and §6.4 is drafted as a recovery provision. Read together, the documents limit every Article IX claim (other than actual fraud) to the $4,200,000 escrow. That includes:
  - title to the Shares and capitalization (§4.3);
  - authority (§4.2);
  - Taxes (§4.13) and Pre-Closing Taxes (§9.2(c));
  - breaches of covenants (§9.2(b));
  - unpaid Closing Indebtedness (§9.2(d)); and
  - Equipment Affiliate creditor claims (§9.2(e)).
- **The negotiated position is lost.** On those claims Paibon bargained for exposure up to $42,000,000 (and the covenant, indebtedness and §9.2(e) claims were never subject to the §9.6(a) cap). The practical loss is up to about **$37,800,000** of recovery capacity.
- **After release, recovery falls to zero.** The escrow is released 18 months after Closing (on or about February 14, 2028, Escrow Agt §5.1). Fundamental Representations survive until 60 days after the statute of limitations (SPA §9.1(a)). After release, §6.4 arguably leaves Paibon with no source of recovery at all for a tax or title claim made in years three to six. Those are exactly the claims the long survival period was meant to protect.
- **The tax exposure is real.** The Company is a member of Seller's consolidated group (SPA §4.13). Pre-Closing Taxes, including several (Treas. Reg. §1.1502-6) liability for other members' consolidated return taxes, are a well-known exposure in a carve-out stock deal.
- **Paibon's counter-argument is not reliable.** Paibon could argue that the §11.9 exception covers only recovery *from* the Escrow Funds, so §6.4 cannot cut off direct recovery from Seller under SPA §9.5. Seller would answer that §6.4 deals expressly with the escrow as the "exclusive source," which falls within the exception. It would also note that Paibon signed the Escrow Agreement after the SPA, on July 28, 2026, which supports reading §6.4 as a deliberate later modification. Paibon should not rely on winning this point.

**Recommended fix (before Closing)**
1. **Amend Escrow Agreement §6.4** to read along these lines: "The Escrow Funds shall be the first, but not the exclusive, source of recovery for claims under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement. Nothing in this Escrow Agreement limits Buyer's right to recover directly from Seller as provided in Sections 9.5 and 9.6 of the Purchase Agreement, including for Fundamental Representations, Pre-Closing Taxes, fraud and claims under Sections 9.2(b)–(e)." Make a conforming change to §6.5 ("...has no further obligation *of the Escrow Agent*...").
2. **As a backstop, amend SPA §11.9** so that the Escrow Agreement controls only the mechanics of release and disbursement. The SPA should control on the scope, amount and sources of recovery, including §§9.5 and 9.6.
3. **Process.** The amendment requires Buyer, Seller and Ostrander to sign (Escrow Agt §10.2). Ostrander should be indifferent, because the change affects only Buyer and Seller.
4. **If Seller refuses,** consider:
   - a larger or longer-lived tax and title holdback;
   - a Seller parent guarantee of direct liability; or
   - R&W insurance with a Fundamental and tax tower.

---

### Issue 2: Larkfield change-of-control consent is not a Required Consent, and §9.2(f) bars indemnity if Larkfield terminates

**Where it appears**
- **SPA Schedule 4.10, item 1.** The Hospital Linen Services Agreement with Larkfield Regional Health System is the Company's largest customer by 2025 revenue. Under its §14.3, Larkfield "may terminate the agreement upon a change of control of the Company unless the customer's prior written consent is obtained."
- **SPA §7.2(d) and Schedule 7.2(d).** The only "Required Consent" is the Stockton Plant landlord's consent.
- **SPA §9.2(f).** Seller is not liable "for any Losses arising out of the failure to obtain any consent, approval or waiver disclosed on the Disclosure Schedules."

**Why it matters for Paibon**
- **Larkfield's termination right is triggered.** Selling 100% of the Shares is a change of control of the Company.
- **Paibon cannot refuse to close on this ground.** Because Larkfield is not on Schedule 7.2(d), Paibon has no condition it can rely on to walk away or delay. Seller's §6.4 efforts covenant also extends only to the Required Consents.
- **No other representation or condition covers it.**
  - §4.4 (No Conflicts) is qualified by the disclosure.
  - §4.17 (Customers) covers only written notice of intent to terminate that has already been received.
  - The §7.2(c) MAE condition is unlikely to be triggered by a consent that has not yet been acted on.
- **Paibon has no recourse after Closing.** If Larkfield terminates, §9.2(f) bars indemnity because the consent was disclosed.
- **The commercial stakes are high.** Paibon would pay $42,000,000 with its largest revenue relationship terminable at the customer's option and no protection. A hospital customer could also use the termination right to renegotiate pricing even if it never terminates.
- **The email thread confirms the gap.** It tracks only the landlord consent (executed and accepted as satisfactory on August 12). Nothing indicates that anyone has approached Larkfield.

**Recommended fix (before Closing)**
1. **Add Larkfield's written consent (or waiver of §14.3) to Schedule 7.2(d)** as a Required Consent, in form reasonably satisfactory to Buyer. This also brings it within Seller's §6.4 efforts covenant and the §3.2(a)(v) deliverables.
2. **Carve Larkfield out of §9.2(f)** and add a **specific indemnity** for Losses (including lost profits or a diminution-in-value formula) if Larkfield terminates or adversely amends its agreement within a set period (for example, 24 months) after Closing. Fund it with a separate holdback or escrow that sits outside the $4,200,000 cap and the §9.6(c) basket.
3. **If Seller will not agree,** consider a price adjustment or earn-out tied to Larkfield's retention. Paibon could also decline to close and rely on the September 30, 2026 outside date, but only if commercially acceptable, because there is no contractual walk right on this point.

**Facts to confirm**
- Larkfield's annual revenue and margin contribution.
- The full text of Larkfield agreement §14.3, including whether it requires notice, whether consent may be unreasonably withheld, the termination notice period, and any termination fees.
- Whether Seller or the Company has already approached Larkfield.

---

### Issue 3: Environmental representations expire before the Phase II investigation must be completed

**Where it appears**
- **SPA §9.1(b).** The §4.14 Environmental Matters representations (wastewater discharge compliance, storage of Hazardous Materials, and no soil or groundwater contamination at the Stockton Plant) survive only until "one hundred eighty (180) days after the Closing Date." Measured from August 14, 2026, that is **February 10, 2027**.
- **SPA §6.7.** Buyer may run a post-closing **Phase II** subsurface investigation (soil and groundwater sampling) and must complete it within **270 days after the Closing Date**, which is **May 11, 2027**.
- **SPA §9.1 (last sentence).** Claims are barred after the survival period unless a written notice "describing the claim in reasonable detail" was delivered before it expired.

**Why it matters for Paibon**
- **The investigation is timed to finish after the representations expire.** The Phase II is the tool Paibon would use to find a breach of §4.14(c), and the contract contemplates that it may finish about three months after expiry.
- **Delaware will enforce the shorter period.** Delaware courts treat an express survival period as a contractual limitations period. Any contamination the Phase II reveals after February 10, 2027 is therefore likely to be time-barred.
- **A protective claim notice is a weak workaround.** Paibon could send a notice before expiry, but a notice sent without sampling data may not meet the "reasonable detail" standard.
- **The exposure is real for this kind of site.** An industrial laundry handling solvents, detergents and bleaching agents carries recognised soil and groundwater risk. Remediation costs can be large and long-tailed.
- **Recovery is limited even for timely claims.** Environmental claims sit under the §9.6(a) $4,200,000 cap and the $315,000 tipping basket (§9.6(c)). Issue 1 limits them further to whatever remains in the escrow.

**Recommended fix (before Closing)**
1. **Amend §9.1(b)** so the §4.14 representations survive at least **36 months** after Closing, or until **90 days after Seller receives the final Phase II report** if later. A claim notice delivered within that period should preserve the claim.
2. **Alternatively or additionally,** add a stand-alone indemnity for pre-Closing contamination at the Stockton Plant identified by the Phase II. It should have its own survival period, sit outside the §9.6(a) cap and the basket, and be backed by an escrow tranche that stays in place past the 18-month release.
3. **As a practical measure,** commission the Phase II consultant now so that fieldwork can begin immediately after Closing, in case Seller will not move the survival date.

**Facts to confirm**
- Whether Paibon has a Phase I ESA and any recognised environmental conditions (RECs).
- The Stockton Plant's wastewater discharge and pretreatment permit history.
- Whether the Stockton Plant Lease places remediation responsibility on the tenant (that is, the Company).

---

### Issue 4: The Section 338(h)(10) election notice window expired on July 16, 2026

**Where it appears**
- **SPA §6.11.** Seller must join in a §338(h)(10) election and deliver an executed IRS Form 8023 at Closing only if Buyer gave written notice "no later than forty-five (45) days after the Signing Date." Otherwise "Seller's obligations under this Section 6.11 shall lapse and be of no further force or effect."
- **Preamble.** The Signing Date was June 1, 2026, so the window **closed on July 16, 2026**. That was before the Escrow Agreement was signed (July 28, 2026) and well before Closing.

**Why it matters for Paibon**
- **The election was available.** Buyer is taxed as a corporation (SPA §5.2) and the Company is a member of Seller's consolidated group (§4.13). A §338(h)(10) election would give the Company a stepped-up tax basis in its assets. That matters most for the tunnel washers, flatwork ironers and route trucks, which are depreciable and are being conveyed into the Company under the Bill of Sale. The resulting depreciation deductions are value Paibon would ordinarily price into a $42,000,000 deal.
- **The right appears to be gone.** The folder contains no election notice. The closing checklist and email thread do not mention Form 8023 or the election, and Form 8023 is not among Seller's §3.2(a) deliverables. On the documents as they stand, Seller's obligation has lapsed. The election requires Seller's joinder, so Paibon cannot make it alone.

**Recommended fix**
1. **First, confirm whether written notice was in fact delivered** to Seller on or before July 16, 2026, in a manner that complies with SPA §11.1. Check the client's files and with Theo Lindqvist. If it was, add Form 8023 to the closing checklist and ask Seller to confirm it will be delivered at Closing.
2. **If no notice was given, negotiate an SPA amendment before Closing** under §11.3. The amendment should:
   - reinstate Seller's obligation to join the election (federal and corresponding state);
   - require delivery of an executed Form 8023 at Closing; and
   - add Form 8023 to §3.2(a).
3. **Expect Seller to ask for compensation.** The election can increase Seller's tax cost, for example by triggering depreciation recapture in the consolidated group. Seller may seek a gross-up or price increase. Paibon's tax advisers should quantify the net present value of the step-up so we know how much Paibon can offer.
4. **Note the filing deadline.** Even with an amendment, Form 8023 must be filed by the 15th day of the 9th month after the month that includes the acquisition date. For an August 2026 acquisition, that is May 15, 2027.

---

### Issue 5: The Escrow Agreement's New York law and Manhattan forum conflict with the SPA's Delaware law and Court of Chancery forum

**Where it appears**
- **Escrow Agreement §10.4.** The Escrow Agreement is governed by "the laws of the State of New York," with exclusive jurisdiction in "the state and federal courts located in the Borough of Manhattan" for any action relating to the Escrow Agreement or the Escrow Funds.
- **Escrow Agreement §2.1 ("Final Order").** A Final Order must come from "a court of competent jurisdiction, as described in Section 10.4."
- **Escrow Agreement §§6.3(c) and 7.5.** Disputed amounts are released only on Joint Written Instructions or a Final Order. Any interpleader action must also be brought in a §10.4 court.
- **SPA §§11.6 and 11.7.** The SPA chooses Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the Delaware Court of Chancery.
- **SPA §11.9.** The Escrow Agreement controls release of and recovery from the Escrow Funds.

**Why it matters for Paibon**
- **Two forums could be needed for one dispute.** Any contested indemnity claim may have to be litigated twice:
  - liability under SPA Article IX in Chancery; and
  - release of the escrow in Manhattan.
  This raises the risk of inconsistent rulings, higher costs and delay.
- **A Delaware judgment may not release the funds.** Because a "Final Order" is tied to a §10.4 court, Ostrander may refuse to release funds on the strength of a Chancery judgment. Paibon would then need a second, New York action.
- **Seller can choose the more favourable forum.** For example, Seller could start an escrow-release action in New York on the Release Date while Paibon's claim is pending in Delaware.
- **Some damage is already done.** The Escrow Agreement was fully executed on July 28, 2026 (email thread, Aug. 3), so these terms are in effect.

**Recommended fix (before Closing, together with the Issue 1 amendment)**
1. **Amend Escrow Agreement §10.4** so that, at least for disputes between Buyer and Seller (including the merits of any Claim Notice or Objection Notice), the agreement is governed by Delaware law with exclusive jurisdiction in the Court of Chancery, consistent with SPA §§11.6 and 11.7. If Ostrander insists, it may keep New York law and forum for its own rights, duties and interpleader.
2. **Amend the "Final Order" definition** to expressly include a final, non-appealable order of the Delaware Court of Chancery (or the Delaware Superior Court).

---

## 3. Lower-priority points

These are less significant, but should be added to the closing checklist.

1. **Bill of Sale Schedule A is incomplete** (Bill of Sale, Schedule A).
   - **Problem:** Serial numbers, VINs, makes and models, and California plate numbers are all "[●]." Seller's counsel said they would be filled in by August 5. An incomplete schedule risks a dispute over exactly what was conveyed, and the route truck titles cannot be matched to it.
   - **Fix:** Before release of signature pages, check the completed schedule against the certificates of title, the odometer statements and the UCC search results.
2. **Liens on the conveyed equipment** (Bill of Sale §5.2; email thread, Aug. 5).
   - **Problem:** Our searches found two financing statements naming Zanoul Equipment Leasing that cover laundry equipment. Seller has agreed to file the UCC-3 terminations on the morning of Closing, before funds move.
   - **Fix:** Keep the step in the closing-call sequence and obtain file-stamped copies. Claims by creditors of Equipment Affiliate are indemnified under SPA §9.2(e), but Issue 1 currently limits that indemnity to the escrow. The Bill of Sale recites no stated consideration from the Company. If Equipment Affiliate is thinly capitalised, consider whether a fraudulent-transfer challenge is a realistic risk.
3. **Undefined SPA terms** (SPA §1.1).
   - **Problem:** The SPA uses several capitalised terms that are not defined in §1.1: "Closing Indebtedness," "Closing Working Capital," "Material Adverse Effect," "Seller's Knowledge," "Governmental Authority" and "GAAP." Undefined MAE and Closing Indebtedness definitions weaken the §7.2(c) condition and the §2.3 adjustment.
   - **Fix:** Confirm whether these definitions sit in a document not provided. If not, address them in the same SPA amendment.
4. **The 18-month escrow release does not match the longer survival periods** (Escrow Agt §5.1; SPA §9.1).
   - **Problem:** If Issues 1 and 3 are fixed by extending survival rather than by allowing direct recovery, the escrow should either stay in place, at least in part, for the longer periods or be backed by a Seller guarantee.
5. **Blanks in the Escrow Agreement** (Escrow Agt §10.1, Exhibits A and B).
   - **Problem:** Notice addresses, authorised representatives and the fee schedule are blank in our copy.
   - **Fix:** Confirm that the executed version is complete. Exhibit A call-back contacts are needed for Ostrander's wire verification under §5.5.

---

## 4. Missing documents, ambiguities and facts to confirm

**Not in the folder:**
- Executed versions of the SPA and Escrow Agreement. Our copies have blank signature blocks.
- The complete Disclosure Schedules. We have only excerpts of Schedule 4.10 and Schedule 7.2(d).
- The Larkfield Hospital Linen Services Agreement, including §14.3.
- The Stockton Plant Lease and the executed landlord consent.
- Any §338(h)(10) election notice, or confirmation that one was sent.
- Any Phase I ESA, and the Phase II scope or engagement letter.
- The Estimated Closing Statement, the payoff letters and the final funds flow. The thread refers to these but they are not attached.
- The completed Bill of Sale Schedule A and the route truck titles.

**To confirm:**
- **338(h)(10) notice (Issue 4):** whether any written election notice was delivered on or before July 16, 2026.
- **Larkfield (Issue 2):** revenue contribution, the termination mechanics under §14.3, and whether anyone has contacted Larkfield.
- **Environmental (Issue 3):** Phase I findings and the Stockton Plant permit and compliance history.
- **Recovery and tax exposure (Issue 1):** whether Paibon is relying on R&W insurance or a Seller guarantee that would change the analysis.
- **Closing status:** whether Closing has taken place. If it has, every recommendation above becomes a post-closing amendment that needs Seller's (and for the escrow, Ostrander's) agreement, and Paibon will have less leverage.

**Email thread.** The thread is logistics only. It is consistent with the documents on timing, the funds flow ($4,200,000 to Ostrander), W-9s, the landlord consent and UCC-3s, and it raises no independent legal issue. It is useful mainly for what it omits: there is no reference to Larkfield's consent, the §338(h)(10) election or Form 8023, or the Phase II.

---

**Next step.** I suggest we send Seller's counsel (Marcus Ebright, Felton Sayre) a single amendment package covering:
- Escrow Agreement §§6.4, 6.5 and 10.4 and the "Final Order" definition;
- SPA §§9.1(b), 9.2(f), 11.9 and 6.11;
- Schedule 7.2(d); and
- the undefined terms.

The package should go out as soon as possible and in any event before the closing call. I am happy to prepare drafts.

**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Paibon Textile Care Partners, LLC: Acquisition of Kestrin Linen Services, Inc. (Pre-Closing Issues List)
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

## I. Background and Scope

Paibon Textile Care Partners, LLC ("**Paibon**" or "**Buyer**") is buying all outstanding shares of Kestrin Linen Services, Inc. (the "**Company**") from Zanoul Holdings, Inc. ("**Seller**"). The key deal terms are:

- **Purchase Price:** $42,000,000 (SPA § 2.1).
- **Indemnity Escrow Amount:** $4,200,000 (SPA § 2.2(b)), deposited with Ostrander Trust Company, N.A. as Escrow Agent.
- **General indemnity cap:** the Indemnity Escrow Amount, so also $4,200,000 (SPA § 9.6(a)).
- **Closing:** remote, scheduled for **August 14, 2026** (SPA § 3.1).

I reviewed the four documents in the folder:

1. The Stock Purchase Agreement dated June 1, 2026 (the "**SPA**").
2. The agreed-form Bill of Sale from Zanoul Equipment Leasing LLC to the Company.
3. The Indemnity Escrow Agreement dated July 28, 2026.
4. The closing-logistics email thread (August 3–12, 2026).

The issues below are **ranked by severity, with the highest priority first**. For each issue I give its location, why it matters to Paibon, and a recommended fix. Points needing factual confirmation are flagged.

---

## II. Issues (Ranked by Consequence to Paibon)

### 1. Escrow Agreement's "sole and exclusive source of recovery" removes the SPA's uncapped protections for Fundamental Representations and Pre-Closing Taxes

**Where:** Escrow Agreement § 6.4, read with SPA §§ 9.5, 9.6(a)–(b) and 11.9.

**The issue:**

- **The SPA bargain.** SPA § 9.6(a) caps Seller's liability for general rep breaches at the $4,200,000 Indemnity Escrow Amount. SPA § 9.6(b) carves out three categories from that cap, each recoverable up to the full $42,000,000 Purchase Price:
  - breaches of Fundamental Representations (organization, authority, capitalization/title to Shares, taxes, brokers);
  - Pre-Closing Taxes; and
  - fraud.
- **Direct recourse in the SPA.** SPA § 9.5 says Losses are satisfied first from the Escrow Funds and then "directly by Seller" if the escrow is insufficient or has been released.
- **The conflicting escrow language.** Escrow Agreement § 6.4 provides that the Escrow Funds "shall be the **sole and exclusive source of recovery** for all claims of the Buyer Indemnitees under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement, except claims for actual fraud." Escrow Agreement § 6.5 adds that if the funds are insufficient, the Escrow Agent pays what is available "and has no further obligation."
- **Why the SPA does not fix this.** One might assume the SPA prevails, because SPA § 11.9 says the SPA prevails over Ancillary Documents. But § 11.9 contains an express exception: "the Escrow Agreement shall control with respect to the release of and recovery from the Escrow Funds." Section 6.4 is squarely a provision about recovery from the Escrow Funds. Seller will argue that the exception applies and that Escrow Agreement § 6.4 governs.

**Why it matters:**

- Only the fraud carve-out survives § 6.4. The Fundamental Representation and Pre-Closing Tax carve-outs are effectively eliminated.
- Paibon's recovery for a title-to-Shares defect, a capitalization problem, or an unpaid pre-closing consolidated-group tax would be limited to the $4,200,000 escrow, not the $42,000,000 Purchase Price.
- **Exposure after the escrow is released.** Fundamental Representations survive until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations (SPA § 9.1(a)). The escrow, however, releases 18 months after Closing (Escrow Agreement § 5.1), on or about February 14, 2028.
  - If § 6.4 controls, a Fundamental Representation or tax claim arising after that date may have no source of recovery at all.
  - This is especially serious for taxes. The Company is part of Seller's consolidated group (SPA § 4.13), so it carries several liability exposure for group taxes.
- The Escrow Agreement was signed July 28, 2026. This is a live executed document, not a draft.

**Recommended fix (before Closing):**

- **Preferred:** amend Escrow Agreement § 6.4 to read: "The Escrow Funds shall be the first, but not the exclusive, source of recovery … Nothing in this Escrow Agreement limits Seller's liability under Section 9.6(b) of the Purchase Agreement or Buyer's right to recover directly from Seller under Section 9.5 of the Purchase Agreement." Conform § 6.5 so that it limits only the Escrow Agent's obligations, not Seller's.
- **Note on amendment mechanics:** Escrow Agreement § 10.2 requires signature by Buyer, Seller *and* the Escrow Agent. Ostrander needs to be brought in immediately.
- **Alternatively or additionally:** amend SPA § 11.9 (signed by Buyer and Seller under SPA § 11.3) so that the Escrow Agreement controls only the *mechanics* of release from the Escrow Funds. The SPA would control on the scope and limits of Seller's liability, including §§ 9.5 and 9.6(b).
- **Fallback:** if Seller resists, Paibon should consider declining to close until this is resolved. Seller may argue that § 6.4 reflects the agreed deal, but the SPA text shows otherwise.

---

### 2. The Section 338(h)(10) election notice window has expired

**Where:** SPA § 6.11, read with the SPA Preamble (Signing Date) and the overall folder.

**The issue:**

- SPA § 6.11 obliges Seller to join in a § 338(h)(10) election, and to deliver an executed IRS Form 8023 at Closing, only if Buyer gives written notice "no later than **forty-five (45) days after the Signing Date**."
- The Signing Date is June 1, 2026, so the window **closed on July 16, 2026**.
- Section 6.11 states that if no timely notice is given, Seller's obligations "shall lapse and be of no further force or effect."
- The folder contains no election notice. Other indicators point the same way:
  - The Escrow Agreement, dated July 28, 2026 (after the window closed), does not mention the election.
  - The closing checklist discussion in the email thread lists the deliverables in detail (W-9, stock powers, officer's certificate, Bill of Sale, resignations) but never mentions Form 8023.
  - On the face of the record, the window was missed.

**Why it matters:**

- The parties are otherwise eligible for the election:
  - Seller is the common parent of a consolidated group that includes the Company (SPA § 4.13).
  - Buyer is classified as a corporation for tax purposes (SPA § 5.2).
- A § 338(h)(10) election gives the Company a stepped-up tax basis in its assets, including the laundry equipment and route fleet. The newly conveyed tunnel washers, flatwork ironers and trucks are depreciable assets where the step-up produces near-term deductions.
- Buyer would ordinarily price that benefit into a $42,000,000 deal. Without Seller's joinder (Form 8023 must be signed by both parties), the election cannot be made, and Paibon takes carryover basis.
- The window cannot be reopened unilaterally. Seller has no contractual obligation to cooperate.

**Recommended fix (before Closing):**

- **Confirm the facts first.** Check with the client (Theo Lindqvist) and the deal team whether any written notice was in fact delivered to Seller on or before July 16, 2026, under the SPA § 11.1 notice mechanics (personal delivery, overnight courier, or email with confirmation). If it was, obtain a copy and add Form 8023 to the Seller closing deliverables.
- **If no timely notice was given,** negotiate a written amendment under SPA § 11.3, before the August 14, 2026 Closing, that:
  - reinstates Seller's obligation to join in the election;
  - requires delivery of an executed Form 8023 (and any state equivalents) at Closing; and
  - addresses allocation and any gross-up.
- **Expect Seller to ask for consideration.** The election can increase Seller-side tax. The client should quantify the value of the step-up so we know how much it can concede.
- **Do not treat the right as still available.** If no amendment is obtained, Paibon should close on the footing that the election right has lapsed.

### 3. Environmental representations expire before the Phase II investigation must be completed

**Where:** SPA § 9.1(b), read with SPA §§ 4.14 and 6.7.

**The issue:**

- SPA § 4.14 contains the environmental representations, which cover the Stockton Plant's:
  - wastewater discharge and pretreatment compliance;
  - storage of detergents, solvents and bleaching agents; and
  - soil and groundwater condition.
- SPA § 9.1(b) provides that these representations survive only until "**one hundred eighty (180) days after the Closing Date**." Measured from August 14, 2026, that is **February 10, 2027**.
- SPA § 6.7 gives Buyer post-closing access for a Phase II subsurface investigation, including soil and groundwater sampling. That investigation need only be completed within **270 days after the Closing Date**, which is **May 11, 2027**.
- Section 9.1 also bars any rep claim brought after the survival period unless a reasonably detailed written claim notice was delivered first.

**Why it matters:**

- The Phase II is the very tool Paibon would use to discover § 4.14(c) contamination. The contract lets that investigation run roughly three months past the date the representations expire.
- Under Delaware law, which governs the SPA (§ 11.6), courts generally enforce an express contractual survival period as a limitation on the time to bring claims.
- Any contamination identified in a Phase II report delivered after February 10, 2027 would very likely be time-barred.
- Industrial laundries carry known solvent and wastewater contamination risk, so this is a material exposure.
- A protective "placeholder" claim notice delivered before February 10, 2027 without Phase II data may not meet the "reasonable detail" standard in § 9.1.

**Recommended fix:**

- Amend SPA § 9.1(b) to extend survival of the § 4.14 representations to at least **36 months after the Closing Date**. Alternatively, tie survival to the later of (i) 18 months after Closing and (ii) a fixed period (e.g., 12 months) after delivery of the final Phase II report.
- Conform the related provisions:
  - Consider whether a portion of the escrow should be held beyond the 18-month Release Date for environmental claims, given Issue 1.
  - Consider whether environmental Losses should sit outside the $315,000 basket (SPA § 9.6(c)).
- **Interim protection:** if Seller will not move, Paibon should instruct its consultant to accelerate the Phase II so that results are available well before February 10, 2027. The client should be told this is a mitigation, not a cure.

### 4. Governing law and forum mismatch between the SPA and the Escrow Agreement

**Where:** Escrow Agreement § 10.4, against SPA §§ 11.6, 11.7 and 11.9.

**The issue:**

- The SPA chooses:
  - Delaware law (§ 11.6); and
  - the exclusive jurisdiction of the **Delaware Court of Chancery**, or the Delaware Superior Court as a fallback (§ 11.7).
- The Bill of Sale is consistent with the SPA (Delaware law and forum, Bill of Sale §§ 8.2–8.3).
- The Escrow Agreement, by contrast, is governed by "the **laws of the State of New York**." It gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state and federal courts "located in the **Borough of Manhattan**" for any action "arising out of or relating to this Escrow Agreement or the Escrow Funds."
- Final Orders (Escrow Agreement § 2.1) and interpleader actions (§ 7.5) are tied to the § 10.4 courts.

**Why it matters:**

- Under SPA § 11.9, the Escrow Agreement controls release of and recovery from the Escrow Funds.
- A disputed indemnity claim could therefore split into two proceedings:
  - a Delaware Chancery action on liability under SPA Article IX; and
  - a New York action over release of the escrow.
- That split risks inconsistent rulings, duplicate cost and delay.
- It also invites Seller to forum-shop. For example, Seller could rush to Manhattan for a declaration on § 6.4 (Issue 1) under New York law, while Paibon proceeds in Chancery.
- Because the Escrow Agent pays disputed amounts only on Joint Written Instructions or a "Final Order" from a § 10.4 court, a Delaware judgment may not by itself compel a release.

**Recommended fix:**

- Amend Escrow Agreement § 10.4 to provide Delaware law and Court of Chancery jurisdiction, at least for disputes between Buyer and Seller.
- Amend the "Final Order" definition so that a final order of the Delaware Court of Chancery (or Superior Court) suffices for release.
- If Ostrander insists on New York law and forum for claims involving its own duties, accept a two-tier clause:
  - New York for claims by or against the Escrow Agent; and
  - Delaware for Buyer–Seller disputes, including entitlement to Escrow Funds.
- This amendment can be combined with the Issue 1 amendment, since both require Ostrander's signature under § 10.2.
